title: Speak Clearly
description: Pronunciation, vocabulary and sentence structure — the building blocks of being understood the first time.

modules.title: Be understood
modules.goal: Clear words beat a perfect accent. Stress the right syllable and finish every word.

lessons.title: Word stress
lessons.summary: Stress the right syllable: deVELopment, PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy.
concept: In English, one syllable in each word is longer, louder and higher. Listeners recognise words by that stress pattern before they process the individual sounds.
Put the stress on the wrong syllable and a perfectly pronounced word can still be misheard — 'deVELopment' said as 'DEvelopment' makes people work to decode you.
Word families shift stress: PHOtograph → phoTOgraphy → photoGRAPHic. Nouns and verbs can differ too: a REcord vs to reCORD.

steps.label: Find it
steps.desc: Look up the stressed syllable (click any word in the drill to see it in CAPITALS).

steps.label: Stretch it
steps.desc: Make the stressed syllable longer, louder and slightly higher.

steps.label: Relax the rest
steps.desc: Unstressed syllables get shorter and softer, often 'uh'.

cheat_sheet: -tion / -sion: stress the syllable before (inforMAtion, deCIsion).
-ity / -ical / -graphy: stress the syllable before (abiLIty, TECHnical, phoTOgraphy).
Two-syllable nouns usually stress the 1st (PROject); verbs the 2nd (proJECT).
Unsure? Click the word in the drill and press ▶ to hear it.

example.prompt: “We need to develop a photography plan.”
example.before: We need to DEvelop a PHOtography plan.
example.after: We need to deVELop a phoTOgraphy plan.
example.why: Same sounds, different stress. The second version is understood instantly.

exercise.instructions: Read each sentence aloud. Exaggerate the stressed syllable of the highlighted words.
exercise.constraint: Read at a natural pace — don't spell words out.

lessons.title: Say technical words clearly
lessons.summary: Long technical words are where speakers mumble. Every syllable counts.
concept: Under pressure we speed up on exactly the words that matter most: the long technical ones.
'Asynchronous', 'idempotent', 'observability' each have four or more syllables. Swallow one and the listener loses the word — and often the sentence.
The fix is mechanical: slow down on the long word, hit its stressed syllable, and finish the ending.

steps.label: Slow
steps.desc: Drop your pace by about 10% on long words only.

steps.label: Stress
steps.desc: Land the stressed syllable (ay-SIHNG-kruh-nuhs).

steps.label: Finish
steps.desc: Say the last sound before moving on.

cheat_sheet: Count the syllables: if a word has 4+, slow down on it.
Never drop the middle syllable: ob-ser-va-BIL-i-ty.
Pause briefly before a key term to give it weight.

example.why: All four syllables, stress on the second.

exercise.instructions: Read each sentence. Slow down on the highlighted technical words.
exercise.constraint: Every syllable of every highlighted word.

lessons.title: Finish your words
concept: When we rush, word endings disappear: 'asked' becomes 'ask', 'costs' becomes 'cost'. That changes tense and number — and meaning.
Endings are also where clusters of consonants pile up (-sts, -kts, -nths). They need a deliberate, tiny bit of time.
Listeners won't notice when you say them. They will notice when you don't.

steps.label: Notice
steps.desc: Spot the -ed, -s and consonant clusters before you speak.

steps.label: Land
steps.desc: Say the final sound fully before the next word.

steps.label: Link
steps.desc: If the next word starts with a vowel, link into it: 'asked_about'.

cheat_sheet: -ed has three sounds: /t/ (asked), /d/ (played), /id/ (wanted).
Plural -s after t/k/p is /s/; after vowels and voiced sounds it's /z/.
Clusters like 'costs' and 'months': slow down, don't simplify.

example.why: Past tense and plural survive — the sentence means what you meant.

exercise.instructions: Read each sentence and land the final sound of every highlighted word.

modules.title: Tricky sounds
modules.goal: Fix the sound swaps that most often cause misunderstandings.

lessons.title: TH sounds
lessons.summary: think, not sink · this, not dis.
concept: TH doesn't exist in many languages, so it's often replaced with s, t, d, f or z: 'think' becomes 'sink' or 'tink'.
There are two TH sounds. Voiceless TH (think, three) is only air. Voiced TH (this, they) adds a buzz from your throat.
Both start the same way: the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth.

steps.label: Tongue
steps.desc: Tip of the tongue lightly between the teeth.

steps.label: Air
steps.desc: Blow air over the tongue: think, three, through.

steps.label: Buzz
steps.desc: Add your voice for this, they, together.

cheat_sheet: Use a mirror: you should see the tip of your tongue.
Minimal pairs: think/sink, three/free, they/day, then/den.
Practise slowly first; speed comes later.

example.before: I sink tree tings went trough.
example.after: I THink THree THings went THrough.
example.why: Every TH audible — no word swaps.

exercise.instructions: Read each sentence. Show your tongue on every TH.
exercise.constraint: No TH turned into s, t, d or f.

lessons.title: V and W
lessons.summary: very, not wery · west, not vest.
concept: V and W are made in completely different places, but many speakers merge them.
V: top teeth gently on the bottom lip, with a buzz. W: round your lips like 'oo' — no teeth at all.
Getting these right makes 'very well' and 'we will review the video' crisp instead of blurred.

steps.label: V = teeth
steps.desc: Top teeth on bottom lip, buzz: very, video, value.

steps.label: W = lips
steps.desc: Round lips, start like 'oo': we, will, work.

steps.label: Alternate
steps.desc: very well · we value · wine vine — slowly, then faster.

cheat_sheet: Touch your lip with your finger: V buzzes against it, W doesn't touch.
Pairs: vest/west, vine/wine, very/wary, verse/worse.

example.prompt: “Very well, we will review the video.”
example.before: Wery vell, ve vill review the wideo.
example.after: Very well, we will review the video.
example.why: V where it's spelled V, W where it's spelled W.

exercise.instructions: Read each sentence. Teeth on lip for V; rounded lips for W.

lessons.title: R and L
lessons.summary: right vs light · correct vs collect.
concept: L touches: the tongue tip presses just behind the top teeth. R doesn't touch anything: the tongue pulls back and the lips round slightly.
Swapping them can change the word entirely — 'collect' vs 'correct', 'play' vs 'pray'.
Slow alternation drills (la-ra-la-ra) build the muscle memory faster than reading lists.

steps.label: L = touch
steps.desc: Tongue tip behind the top teeth: light, leader, reliable.

steps.label: R = float
steps.desc: Tongue pulled back, touching nothing: right, release.

steps.label: Alternate
steps.desc: la-ra-la-ra, light-right, collect-correct.

cheat_sheet: Pairs: right/light, road/load, pray/play, correct/collect, grass/glass.
Words with both are the real test: 'reliable', 'rollout', 'relationships'.

example.why: The swap in the 'before' reverses the meaning.

exercise.instructions: Read each sentence. Feel the tongue touch on L and float on R.

modules.title: Words & sentences
modules.goal: Choose precise words and build sentences that are easy to follow.

lessons.title: Upgrade your words
lessons.summary: Swap vague words (good, thing, a lot) for precise ones — and use today's words.
concept: Articulate speakers don't use longer words; they use more precise ones. 'It was really good' tells the listener nothing. 'It cut costs by a third' tells them everything.
Vague words are placeholders: good, bad, thing, stuff, a lot, very. Each one is a chance to say exactly what you mean.
Building vocabulary works best in use, not in lists. That's why the app gives you three words a day to use in real answers.

steps.label: Precise
steps.desc: Replace vague words: good → effective, thing → risk/factor/issue.

steps.label: Specific
steps.desc: Add the number, name or example the vague word was hiding.

steps.label: Fresh
steps.desc: Use at least one of today's words naturally.

cheat_sheet: very important → critical · a lot of → significant · big → major
deal with → handle / resolve · make sure → ensure
Don't force fancy words: precise beats impressive.

example.before: It went really good, we got a lot of users and stuff.
example.after: It exceeded our target — 12,000 sign-ups in the first week, mostly from the referral campaign.
example.why: Every vague word became a fact.

exercise.instructions: Answer with zero vague words, and use at least one of today's words.
prompts: What are you most proud of in the last year?
Describe a project that failed or slipped. What was your part in it?
How would your team describe your working style?
exercise.constraint: No good / bad / thing / stuff / a lot. One of today's words.

checks.label: At most one weak word or phrase

lessons.title: Vary your sentences
lessons.summary: Break run-ons, mix short and long sentences, and change your openers.
concept: Spoken run-ons ('and then… and so… and then…') are the most common structure problem. The listener can't tell where one idea ends.
Strong speakers vary rhythm: a long sentence that explains, then a short one that lands. Like this.
Starting every sentence with 'So' or 'I' makes speech sound flat. Vary your openers: 'Because…', 'The result…', 'Last year…'.

steps.label: Stop
steps.desc: End the sentence instead of saying 'and'. Pause.

steps.label: Mix
steps.desc: Follow a long sentence with a short one.

steps.label: Open
steps.desc: Vary the first word of each sentence.

cheat_sheet: If you hear yourself say 'and then', stop and start a new sentence.
Aim for 10–20 words per sentence on average.
Use 'because', 'which' and 'although' to connect ideas without chaining.

example.before: So the brokers ran out of disk and then we got paged and so we restarted them and then it was fine.
example.after: Two brokers ran out of disk at 2 a.m. We were paged within a minute. Because the restart fixed it, we added disk alerts that afternoon.
example.why: Three clear sentences, varied openers, one 'because' instead of four 'and's.

exercise.instructions: Answer in short, complete sentences. No 'and then' chains.
prompts: Give an update to leadership on a project that is two weeks behind.
Explain to your team why you're changing the on-call process.
Walk me through how your team handled its last incident.
exercise.constraint: No run-ons. Start sentences with different words.

lessons.title: Active, clean sentences
lessons.summary: Say who did what. Fewer passives, no grammar slips.
concept: 'Mistakes were made' hides who made them. 'I missed the deadline' owns it. Active voice sounds confident and is easier to follow.
Passive voice has its place (when the actor doesn't matter), but in interviews and updates it often blurs ownership.
Small grammar slips — 'he don't', 'there's many', 'less people' — distract listeners from your point.

steps.label: Who
steps.desc: Start with the actor: I, we, the team, the system.

steps.label: Did
steps.desc: A strong verb: built, decided, cut, shipped.

steps.label: What
steps.desc: The object or result: the pipeline, the cost, the deadline.

cheat_sheet: 'was decided' → 'we decided' · 'was built by me' → 'I built'.
'there's many' → 'there are many' · 'less people' → 'fewer people'.
'he don't' → 'he doesn't'.

example.before: The migration was delayed and some issues was found and a decision was made to roll back.
example.after: We delayed the migration after QA found two issues. I decided to roll back.
example.why: Actors are clear, verbs are active, and the grammar slip is gone.

exercise.instructions: Use active voice: start sentences with who acted.
prompts: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a senior stakeholder.
Tell me about the hardest technical problem you solved in the last year.
Describe a decision you made with incomplete information.
exercise.constraint: At most one passive. No grammar slips.
